docs.title: How to read dependencies
docs.text:
• Required means the documented service configuration expects that dependency for the specified deployment.
  • Optional means an integration or feature is enabled only when configured.
  • Runtime dependency means a workload may fail when a service is unavailable.
  • Management integration means a service may continue running but lose policy updates, lineage, audits, or UI functionality.

Always verify with the official service dependency documentation for the exact release: https://docs.cloudera.com/cdp-private-cloud-base/7.3.2/cdp-private-cloud-base-installation/topics/cdpdc-service-dependencies.html

docs.title: HDFS: Architecture, Components, Dependencies, and Operations
1. Purpose
docs.text: HDFS is the distributed file system used to store large files across DataNodes with fault tolerance. The NameNode manages namespace metadata; DataNodes store block replicas.

docs.title: 2. Main components and roles
docs.text: Component / role Responsibility NameNode Maintains HDFS namespace metadata, file-to-block mappings, permissions, and block-location knowledge; does not store file payload bytes. Standby NameNode (HA) Tracks shared namespace edits and maintains a synchronized namespace so it can take over during failover. DataNode Stores and serves HDFS block replicas, sends heartbeats/block reports, and participates in replication and write pipelines. JournalNode (QJM HA) Persists shared edit-log transactions for NameNode HA; the Active writes to a quorum and Standby tails the edits. ZKFC Monitors local NameNode health and participates in automatic failover coordination and fencing. checkpoint role (Secondary NameNode/CheckpointNode/Standby depending on architecture) Creates checkpoints by combining namespace image state with later edits; a Secondary NameNode is not automatically a hot standby. HDFS client. Core responsibility depends on the configured role and CDP release; verify the role description in Cloudera Manager and the official versioned guide.

docs.title: Role
docs.text: A DataNode stores HDFS block replicas on local disks and serves read/write requests. It reports liveness through heartbeats and inventories through block reports.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Store block files and associated metadata/checksums.
  • Serve client reads.
  • Participate in write pipelines.
  • Replicate blocks when instructed.
  • Delete replicas when instructed.
  • Report disk/storage health and block inventory.

docs.title: Failure behavior
docs.text: If a DataNode becomes unavailable, clients may read from another replica. The NameNode detects missed heartbeats and may schedule re-replication if valid replicas remain and capacity/policies permit it. If all replicas of a block are lost, the data is unavailable.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
hdfs dfsadmin -report
hdfs fsck /path -files -blocks -locations
Use Cloudera Manager host and DataNode health metrics for disk failures, volume failures, capacity, and heartbeat status.

docs.title: FSImage
docs.text: A persisted snapshot of the NameNode filesystem namespace at a particular transaction point. It contains namespace metadata and file-to-block relationships, not the file's actual bytes.

docs.title: EditLog
docs.text: A sequence of namespace-changing transactions after the checkpoint, such as creating/closing files, mkdir, rename, delete, chmod, or chown.

docs.title: What does not normally create an EditLog transaction?
docs.text:
• hdfs dfs -ls /data/abc.txt — read-only listing.
  • hdfs dfs -get /user/hive/db/abc.txt . — reads HDFS data to local storage.
  • hdfs dfsadmin -report — reports cluster state.

docs.title: What normally changes namespace state?
docs.text:
• hdfs dfs -put local.csv /user/hive/db/ — creates destination namespace/file state and block associations.
  • hdfs dfs -mkdir /data/new — creates directory metadata.
  • hdfs dfs -rm /data/old.csv — removes namespace entry.
  • hdfs dfs -chmod 640 /data/file — changes metadata.

Running -ls five times does not create five EditLog transactions merely because it ran five times. FSImage is not rewritten after each command. Checkpointing merges the prior image and applicable edits to create a newer image.

docs.title: Can FSImage be read as text?
docs.text:
Not directly as a normal text file; it is a structured/binary format. Use the Offline Image Viewer, with syntax verified for your Hadoop version, for example: 

hdfs oiv -i /path/to/fsimage -o /tmp/fsimage.xml -p XML
The offline edits viewer (hdfs oev in supported versions) can inspect edit segments. Never modify NameNode metadata files manually. XML output can be large and sensitive.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: HDFS stores large files across multiple DataNodes. It splits files into blocks and replicates blocks to provide fault tolerance. The NameNode manages the namespace and block-location metadata.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
HDFS client
                               |
                   metadata RPC to NameNode
                               |
                 +-------------+-------------+
                 |                           |
            Active NameNode             Standby NameNode
                 |                           ^
                 | writes edits              | tails shared edits
                 v                           |
           JournalNode quorum (JN1/JN2/JN3 in a typical HA setup)

HDFS client -------------- data stream --------------> DataNodes
                                                    DN1 DN2 DN3
                                                    block replicas

ZKFC on NameNode hosts <---- coordination ----> ZooKeeper ensemble

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Component Responsibility Failure significance NameNode Namespace, inode metadata, file-to-block mapping, block locations, permissions Namespace service unavailable unless HA failover succeeds DataNode Stores and serves block replicas; heartbeats and block reports Replicas may become unavailable; HDFS may re-replicate Standby NameNode Tracks edits and maintains namespace state for failover No ready standby if it falls behind or fails JournalNode Shared edits in QJM HA Loss of quorum can prevent safe namespace edits ZKFC Monitors NameNode and participates in automatic failover Failover automation can be impaired ZooKeeper Coordination/leader-election primitives for HA Quorum loss affects coordination Checkpoint role Merges FSImage and edits into a checkpoint, depending on architecture Checkpoint lag can grow metadata recovery time

docs.title: HDFS read flow
docs.text:
1. Client requests file metadata/block locations from NameNode.
  2. NameNode returns locations for the file's blocks.
  3. Client chooses a suitable replica, typically favoring network locality.
  4. Client reads bytes directly from DataNode.
  5. Client verifies checksums and can retry another replica if a read fails.
  6. Client requests locations for later blocks as needed.

docs.title: HDFS write flow
docs.text:
1. Client requests file creation from NameNode.
  2. NameNode checks permissions, path, and namespace rules.
  3. NameNode selects a DataNode pipeline for a block.
  4. Client streams packets to the first DataNode; it forwards packets down the pipeline.
  5. Acknowledgements return through the pipeline.
  6. On block completion, the client obtains a pipeline for the next block if needed.
  7. Client closes the file; NameNode records the final namespace state.

docs.title: Key distinction
docs.text: The NameNode does not normally proxy file bytes. The client exchanges metadata with the NameNode and streams data directly to/from DataNodes.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
hdfs dfs -ls /data
hdfs dfs -put ./sample.csv /data/
hdfs dfs -get /data/sample.csv .
hdfs dfs -df -h /
hdfs dfsadmin -report
hdfs fsck /data -files -blocks -locations
hdfs haadmin -getServiceState nn1
Check command availability and impact in the target release. Scope fsck carefully on large production filesystems.

docs.title: HDFS HA and ZooKeeper
docs.text:
ZKFC on Active host ----\
                         +---- ZooKeeper ensemble (coordination)
ZKFC on Standby host ---/

Active NameNode ---- writes edits ----> JournalNode quorum
Standby NameNode <--- tails edits ----- JournalNode quorum
  • Active NameNode: serves namespace requests and writes edits.
  • Standby NameNode: stays synchronized and can take over.
  • JournalNodes: shared edits in QJM-based HA.
  • ZKFC: monitors NameNode health and coordinates failover.
  • ZooKeeper: coordination and leader-election primitives.
  • Fencing: prevents the old Active from continuing to serve as Active after failover.

One ZooKeeper down in a three-node ensemble normally leaves quorum (2/3). Two down means no majority, so coordination-dependent behavior is impaired. ZooKeeper and JournalNode quorum are separate concerns.

docs.title: HDFS Read Architecture
docs.text:
Client                 NameNode                   DataNodes
  | -- open(path) -------> |
  | <-- block locations -- |
  | ---------------- read block 0 -------------> DN2
  | <--------------- data bytes ---------------- |
  | ---------------- read block 1 -------------> DN5
  | <--------------- data bytes ---------------- |
  v
Application receives file bytes
  1. Client requests file metadata and block locations.
  2. NameNode returns replica locations, ordered according to placement/locality logic.
  3. Client selects a replica and reads data directly.
  4. Client verifies checksums.
  5. If a replica fails, client may retry another replica and report the bad replica.
  6. NameNode is not in the data path for the file bytes.

Interview point: NameNode outage can prevent new metadata lookups, even though existing established DataNode streams may behave differently depending on timing/client state. Do not claim all active reads instantly stop in every case.

docs.title: HDFS Write Architecture
docs.text:
Client             NameNode                DN1             DN2             DN3
  | -- create(path) --> |
  | <-- pipeline ------- |
  | ---- packet -------> | DN1 --forward--> DN2 --forward--> DN3
  | <--- ACK chain ------|<------ ACK <------- ACK <---------|
  | -- next block request when needed
  | -- close ------------>
  1. Client asks NameNode to create a file.
  2. NameNode checks permissions and namespace constraints.
  3. For each block, NameNode chooses target DataNodes using replication and placement policies.
  4. Client streams packets to the pipeline's first DataNode.
  5. Each DataNode writes and forwards packets; acknowledgements return upstream.
  6. If a pipeline node fails, the client can recover/reconfigure the pipeline according to HDFS protocol.
  7. File close finalizes the write state.

The NameNode chooses metadata and targets; the file payload moves through DataNodes.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: In the common Quorum Journal Manager (QJM) HA design, JournalNodes hold the shared NameNode edit-log stream.

docs.title: Write/read relationship
docs.text:
• Active NameNode writes namespace edits to a JournalNode quorum.
  • Standby NameNode reads/tails edits and applies them to its namespace state.
  • A typical small HA design uses three JournalNodes, requiring a majority for quorum operations.

docs.title: Failure examples
docs.text:
• One of three JNs down: two remain, so quorum usually remains.
  • Two of three JNs down: quorum is lost; Active may be unable to commit namespace edits safely.
  • JournalNodes are not DataNodes and do not store user HDFS blocks.

docs.title: Role
docs.text: The NameNode is the HDFS namespace manager. It tracks directories, file metadata, permissions, file-to-block relationships, and known block locations. It does not store the actual user file bytes.

docs.title: Related state
docs.text:
• FSImage: persisted namespace snapshot.
  • EditLog: namespace-changing transactions after the checkpoint.
  • Block reports: DataNode-provided inventory used to maintain block-location knowledge.
  • Heartbeats: signals that DataNodes are alive.

docs.title: Request flow
docs.text: Client asks to open/create/list a path -> NameNode checks namespace and permissions -> returns metadata/block locations or records a namespace transaction -> client communicates directly with DataNodes for file bytes.

docs.title: HA
docs.text: In an HA setup, Active serves namespace requests and writes edits to shared edits (commonly JournalNodes via QJM). Standby applies those edits to remain ready. ZKFC and ZooKeeper coordinate failover; fencing prevents an old Active from continuing to act as Active.

docs.title: Failure scenarios
docs.text:
• Active down: failover may promote Standby if synchronization, quorum, and fencing are healthy.
  • Standby down: Active may continue but HA redundancy is reduced.
  • NameNode storage full/corrupt: high-severity metadata risk; follow recovery runbooks and preserve metadata copies.
  • DataNode down: NameNode marks it dead after missed heartbeats and may schedule re-replication.

docs.title: Interview question
docs.text: Does the NameNode store the actual file data? No. It manages namespace metadata and block locations; DataNodes store the blocks.

docs.title: YARN: Architecture, Components, Dependencies, and Operations
1. Purpose
docs.text: YARN manages cluster compute resources and schedules application containers.

docs.title: 2. Main components and roles
docs.text: Component / role Responsibility ResourceManager Accepts the Spark application and coordinates YARN resource allocation. Scheduler ResourceManager subcomponent that allocates containers according to configured queues, capacities, priorities, labels, and policies. ApplicationsManager Handles application submission/admission and manages ApplicationMaster lifecycle at the ResourceManager level. NodeManager Runs on worker nodes, launches and monitors containers, manages local resources/logs, and reports node health/resources. ApplicationMaster per application Coordinates one application's execution and negotiates containers from ResourceManager. Container A resource allocation on a NodeManager, typically including memory, vcores, and a launch context. JobHistory is separate for MapReduce history. Core responsibility depends on the configured role and CDP release; verify the role description in Cloudera Manager and the official versioned guide.

docs.title: MapReduce and JobHistory Server: Architecture, Components, Dependencies, and Operations
1. Purpose
docs.text: MapReduce is a batch processing framework with map, shuffle/sort, and reduce phases. JobHistory Server serves historical job details after completion.

docs.title: 2. Main components and roles
docs.text: Component / role Responsibility MR client Submits a MapReduce job and its configuration, jar, and input/output details. ResourceManager Accepts the Spark application and coordinates YARN resource allocation. MRAppMaster Coordinates one MapReduce application, schedules map/reduce tasks, and manages retries and task state. map tasks Read input splits and emit intermediate key/value records. reduce tasks Consume shuffled/sorted intermediate records and produce final output. NodeManager Runs on worker nodes, launches and monitors containers, manages local resources/logs, and reports node health/resources. JobHistory Server Serves historical MapReduce job, task, counter, and attempt information; it is not the live scheduler. history logs. Core responsibility depends on the configured role and CDP release; verify the role description in Cloudera Manager and the official versioned guide.

docs.title: Production Troubleshooting
docs.text: Common production issues, symptoms, investigation commands, root causes, solutions, and prevention.

docs.title: 1. Production Issue
docs.text:
A DataNode is reported as Dead, Down, or Unhealthy.

Example:

Live DataNodes: 31
Dead DataNodes: 1

or Cloudera Manager reports a DataNode health alert.

docs.title: Step 1: Check HDFS DataNodes
docs.text:
hdfs dfsadmin -report

Look for:

Live datanodes
Dead datanodes
Decommissioned datanodes

docs.title: Step 2: Identify the affected DataNode
docs.text:
Note:

Hostname
IP address
Last contact
Configured capacity
DFS used
DFS remaining

docs.title: Step 3: Check whether the server is reachable
docs.text:
ping <datanode-hostname>

Check SSH:

ssh <datanode-hostname>

If SSH is unavailable, investigate the server/infrastructure layer.

docs.title: Step 4: Check server health
docs.text:
On the DataNode:

hostname
uptime
df -h
df -i
free -h

Check CPU:

top

docs.title: Step 5: Check Cloudera Agent
docs.text:
sudo systemctl status cloudera-scm-agent

Check recent agent messages:

sudo journalctl -u cloudera-scm-agent --since "30 minutes ago"

docs.title: Step 6: Check DataNode process
docs.text:
jps

Look for:

DataNode

If the DataNode process is missing, investigate why it stopped.

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
• Server rebooted.
  • Server crashed.
  • Hardware failure.
  • Disk failure.

docs.title: Operating system
docs.text:
• Filesystem full.
  • Inode exhaustion.
  • High memory pressure.
  • OS problem.

docs.title: Hadoop
docs.text:
• DataNode process stopped.
  • Java/JVM problem.
  • DataNode configuration issue.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
• DataNode cannot communicate with NameNode.
  • DNS issue.
  • Firewall/network issue.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Kerberos authentication failure.
  • Incorrect keytab.
  • Expired credentials.

docs.title: Case 1 — DataNode process stopped
docs.text:
Check:

jps

Review DataNode logs and Cloudera Manager health information.

If the service is managed by Cloudera Manager, use Cloudera Manager's Start action for the DataNode role according to your operational procedure.

docs.title: Case 2 — Filesystem is full
docs.text:
Check:

df -h

Check inode usage:

df -i

Identify the cause before removing anything.

docs.title: Case 3 — Disk failure
docs.text:
Check disks:

lsblk

Check kernel messages:

dmesg | grep -Ei "error|fail|I/O|disk"

Follow your infrastructure/hardware replacement procedure.

docs.title: Case 4 — Network issue
docs.text:
Check hostname resolution:

hostname -f
getent hosts <namenode-hostname>

Test connectivity to the required Hadoop service port:

nc -vz <namenode-hostname> <port>

Use the actual configured port for your environment.

docs.title: Case 5 — Kerberos problem
docs.text:
Check:

klist

Test the configured keytab:

kinit -kt /path/to/keytab <principal>

Then:

klist

docs.title: 5. Check DataNode Logs
docs.text:
Search for errors:

grep -i "error" <datanode-log-file>

Disk problems:

grep -Ei "disk|space|volume|failed" <datanode-log-file>

Kerberos problems:

grep -Ei "kerberos|authentication|GSS|SASL" <datanode-log-file>

docs.title: 6. Verification
docs.text:
Run:

hdfs dfsadmin -report

The DataNode should return to the Live DataNodes list.

Also check:

hdfs fsck /

Look for replication problems.

Verify the DataNode health in Cloudera Manager.

docs.title: 7. Production Prevention
docs.text:
• Monitor DataNode heartbeat.
  • Monitor disk health.
  • Monitor disk and inode utilization.
  • Monitor JVM health.
  • Maintain sufficient disk headroom.
  • Monitor network connectivity.
  • Maintain correct Kerberos configuration.

docs.title: 9. Interview Question
docs.text:
Q: A DataNode suddenly becomes dead. What will you check?

I would first confirm the DataNode status with hdfs dfsadmin -report, then check server availability, disk and inode usage, Cloudera Agent, DataNode process, network connectivity, logs and Kerberos. I would identify the root cause before restarting anything and then verify the DataNode and HDFS replication health after recovery.

docs.title: HDFS Disk Full / DataNode Disk Usage High
1. Production Issue
docs.text:
One or more DataNodes are running out of disk space.

Typical situation:

DataNode disk utilization: 90%+
HDFS remaining capacity: very low
Spark jobs failing
HDFS write operations failing
DataNode health alerts

docs.title: Step 1: Check overall HDFS capacity
docs.text:
hdfs dfs -df -h

Check:

  • Total capacity
  • Used capacity
  • Remaining capacity

docs.title: Step 2: Check DataNode utilization
docs.text:
hdfs dfsadmin -report

Look for:

Configured Capacity
DFS Used
DFS Remaining
Non DFS Used

Pay particular attention to DataNodes with significantly higher utilization than others.

docs.title: Step 3: Check the operating-system disk
docs.text:
SSH to the affected DataNode:

ssh <datanode-host>

Then:

df -h

This is important because high disk utilization can come from both:

  • HDFS data
  • Non-HDFS data

docs.title: Step 4: Check inode utilization
docs.text:
df -i

A filesystem can have free GB available but still run out of inodes because of a very large number of files.

docs.title: Step 5: Find large HDFS directories
docs.text:
For example:

hdfs dfs -du -h /

Check specific directories:

hdfs dfs -du -h /user

hdfs dfs -du -h /tmp

hdfs dfs -du -h /user/spark

Identify which directories are consuming the most space.

docs.title: Cause 1 — Large datasets
docs.text: A large amount of new data has been loaded into HDFS.

docs.title: Cause 2 — Old data
docs.text: Old datasets are no longer required but were never removed.

docs.title: Cause 3 — Spark/application temporary data
docs.text: Temporary or staging data is consuming significant space.

docs.title: Cause 4 — High replication factor
docs.text:
For example:

1 TB logical data
Replication factor = 3

Approximate physical HDFS storage = 3 TB

Check replication:

hdfs fsck /path/to/file -files -blocks -locations

docs.title: Cause 5 — Non-HDFS files
docs.text:
Check the DataNode filesystem:

df -h

If OS-level usage is much higher than HDFS usage, investigate non-HDFS directories.

docs.title: Fix 1 — Remove obsolete data
docs.text:
First confirm:

  • Data owner
  • Retention policy
  • Whether the data is still required
  • Whether another copy exists

Then remove confirmed obsolete data:

hdfs dfs -rm -r /path/to/obsolete/data

Never delete production data just because it is large.

docs.title: Fix 2 — Clean unnecessary temporary data
docs.text:
Identify temporary data first:

hdfs dfs -du -h /tmp

Then follow your organization's approved cleanup process.

docs.title: Fix 3 — Reduce replication where appropriate
docs.text:
If business requirements permit a lower replication factor:

hdfs dfs -setrep -w 2 /path/to/data

Verify:

hdfs fsck /path/to/data -files -blocks -locations

Do not reduce replication blindly.

Replication provides data availability and fault tolerance.

docs.title: Fix 4 — Run HDFS Balancer
docs.text:
If the problem is uneven DataNode utilization:

hdfs dfsadmin -report

Then, according to your cluster's approved procedure:

hdfs balancer -threshold 10

The threshold should be selected according to the cluster's operational requirements.

docs.title: Fix 5 — Add DataNode capacity
docs.text:
If the cluster is genuinely running out of capacity and cleanup is insufficient, the long-term solution may be:

Add disks
       OR
Add DataNodes
       OR
Increase storage capacity

docs.title: 5. Verification
docs.text:
After the fix:

hdfs dfs -df -h

Then:

hdfs dfsadmin -report

Check:

  • DataNode utilization
  • Remaining capacity
  • HDFS health
  • Under-replicated blocks

For a targeted check:

hdfs fsck /path/to/data

docs.title: 6. Production Prevention
docs.text:
• Monitor DataNode disk utilization.
  • Maintain disk-usage alert thresholds.
  • Implement data-retention policies.
  • Clean temporary data regularly.
  • Review replication policies.
  • Perform capacity planning.
  • Monitor non-HDFS disk usage.
  • Monitor inode utilization.

docs.title: 7. Production Troubleshooting Flow
docs.text:
Disk usage alert
       ↓
hdfs dfs -df -h
       ↓
hdfs dfsadmin -report
       ↓
Identify affected DataNode
       ↓
df -h / df -i
       ↓
Check HDFS directories
       ↓
Identify root cause
       ↓
Cleanup / replication / balancing / capacity expansion
       ↓
Verify HDFS health

docs.title: 8. Important Commands
docs.text:
hdfs dfs -df -h
hdfs dfsadmin -report
hdfs dfs -du -h /
hdfs fsck /path
hdfs dfs -setrep -w 2 /path
hdfs balancer -threshold 10
df -h
df -i

docs.title: 9. Interview Question
docs.text:
Q: A DataNode is at 90% disk utilization. How will you troubleshoot it?

First check HDFS capacity using hdfs dfs -df -h and hdfs dfsadmin -report. Then identify the affected DataNode and check OS-level disk usage with df -h. Next identify large HDFS directories, temporary data, replication overhead and non-HDFS usage. After identifying the root cause, clean only approved obsolete data, adjust replication if appropriate, balance the cluster, or add capacity. Finally verify the cluster health.

docs.title: 1. Production Issue
docs.text:
A Hadoop command, service, application or user receives a Kerberos authentication error.

Common examples:

Client not found in Kerberos database

Authentication failed

docs.title: Step 1 — Check current ticket

klist

kinit <principal>

klist

docs.text:

kinit -kt /path/to/service.keytab <principal>

klist

klist -kte /path/to/service.keytab

  • Realm
  • Key version number
  • Encryption types

Make sure the expected principal exists.

hostname

hostname -f

date

timedatectl

docs.text: The principal does not match the expected account.

docs.title: Incorrect keytab
docs.text: The keytab is missing, outdated or contains the wrong principal.

docs.title: DNS/hostname mismatch
docs.text: The hostname doesn't match the service principal configuration.

docs.title: Clock synchronization
docs.text: The server's time differs too much from the KDC.

docs.title: KDC unavailable
docs.text: The Kerberos KDC cannot be reached.

docs.title: Fix 1 — Renew user ticket
docs.text:
kdestroy

Then:

kinit <principal>

Verify:

klist

docs.title: Fix 2 — Test service keytab
docs.text:
kinit -kt /path/to/service.keytab <principal>

Then:

klist

If this fails, verify the principal and keytab with the Kerberos/Hadoop administration team.

docs.title: Fix 3 — Correct time synchronization
docs.text:
Check:

timedatectl status

chronyc tracking

Correct time synchronization according to the organization's standard.

docs.title: Fix 4 — Check hostname/DNS
docs.text:
hostname -f

getent hosts <hostname>

Correct DNS/hostname configuration if it doesn't match the deployed Kerberos service principal configuration.

docs.title: Fix 5 — Check KDC connectivity
docs.text:
Check network connectivity to the configured KDC according to your environment.

Do not assume a port or modify firewall rules without confirming the actual Kerberos configuration.

docs.title: 9. Verify Hadoop Access
docs.text:
After obtaining a valid ticket:

klist

Then test:

hdfs dfs -ls /

If successful, the user's Hadoop authentication is working.

For a service, test the actual affected service/application as well.

docs.title: 10. Production Prevention
docs.text:
• Monitor KDC availability.
  • Maintain DNS consistency.
  • Maintain time synchronization.
  • Protect keytabs.
  • Document service principals.
  • Follow keytab rotation procedures.
  • Monitor authentication failures.
  • Maintain correct service configurations.

docs.title: 11. Troubleshooting Flow
docs.text:
Kerberos Error
      ↓
klist
      ↓
Valid ticket?
      ↓
NO → kinit
      ↓
YES → Check principal
      ↓
Keytab problem?
      ↓
klist -kte
      ↓
Check hostname/DNS
      ↓
Check time synchronization
      ↓
Check KDC connectivity
      ↓
Test Hadoop operation

docs.title: 12. Interview Question
docs.text:
Q: A Hadoop user suddenly gets a Kerberos authentication failure. What will you check?

I would first run klist to check the current ticket. If necessary, I would obtain a new ticket using kinit. For service authentication, I would test the keytab using kinit -kt and inspect it with klist -kte. I would then verify the principal, hostname/DNS, time synchronization and KDC connectivity before testing the affected Hadoop operation again.

docs.title: 1. Production Issue
docs.text:
A YARN application is stuck in:

ACCEPTED

or remains in:

RUNNING

for an unexpectedly long time.

docs.title: 2. How to Identify
docs.text:
List running/submitted applications:

yarn application -list

Check the specific application:

yarn application -status <application_id>

Example:

yarn application -status application_123456789_0001

docs.title: 3. If Application Is Stuck in ACCEPTED
docs.text:
An application in ACCEPTED generally means YARN has accepted the application but has not yet launched the ApplicationMaster.

Check NodeManagers:

yarn node -list

Check queue:

yarn queue -status <queue_name>

Review the queue and cluster resource utilization in Cloudera Manager.

docs.title: 4. Common Causes of ACCEPTED
docs.text:
• Insufficient memory.
  • Insufficient CPU.
  • Queue capacity exhausted.
  • Queue/user limits reached.
  • Too many applications already running.
  • NodeManagers unavailable.
  • Application requests very large resources.
  • Queue configuration restrictions.

docs.title: 5. If Application Is RUNNING but Not Progressing
docs.text:
Get application logs:

yarn logs -applicationId <application_id>

Save them:

yarn logs -applicationId <application_id> > application.log

Search for errors:

grep -i "error" application.log

Search for failures:

grep -Ei "exception|failed|killed|timeout" application.log

docs.title: 6. Check YARN Resources
docs.text:
Check NodeManagers:

yarn node -list

Review in Cloudera Manager:

YARN
 ├── Memory utilization
 ├── CPU utilization
 ├── NodeManagers
 ├── Queues
 └── Applications

Check whether the requested application resources are unusually high.

docs.title: Resource starvation
docs.text: Application requests more memory/CPU than currently available.

docs.title: Queue saturation
docs.text: The queue has reached its configured capacity.

docs.title: Application problem
docs.text: The application itself is stuck or failing.

docs.title: Data skew
docs.text: One or more tasks take significantly longer than others.

docs.title: External dependency
docs.text: The application is waiting for another system.

docs.title: Case 1 — Queue is full
docs.text:
Review the queue configuration and running applications.

If appropriate, stop obsolete/stuck applications after confirming ownership.

docs.title: Case 2 — Application has excessive resource requirements
docs.text:
Review the application's memory and CPU configuration.

For Spark-on-YARN, inspect:

spark.executor.memory
spark.executor.cores
spark.executor.instances
spark.driver.memory

Do not reduce production resources blindly; determine the application's actual requirements first.

docs.title: Case 3 — Application is genuinely stuck
docs.text:
After confirming with the application owner:

yarn application -kill <application_id>

Then investigate why the application became stuck before allowing it to run again.

docs.title: 9. Verification
docs.text:
Check:

yarn application -list

Verify the affected application is no longer stuck.

Check:

yarn node -list

Verify NodeManagers are healthy.

Confirm that other applications are receiving resources normally.

docs.title: 10. Prevention
docs.text:
• Monitor queue utilization.
  • Monitor long-running applications.
  • Set appropriate queue capacity.
  • Educate developers on resource sizing.
  • Monitor failed applications.
  • Review Spark executor/driver sizing.
  • Monitor data skew and application performance.

docs.title: 11. Troubleshooting Flow
docs.text:
Application Stuck
       ↓
yarn application -status
       ↓
ACCEPTED or RUNNING?
       ↓
ACCEPTED → Check queue/resources/NodeManagers
       ↓
RUNNING → Check logs/tasks/resources
       ↓
Identify root cause
       ↓
Fix configuration/application/queue
       ↓
Kill only if approved
       ↓
Verify application and YARN health

docs.title: 12. Interview Question
docs.text:
Q: A YARN application has been in ACCEPTED state for 30 minutes. What will you check?

I would check the application's requested resources, YARN queue capacity, available cluster resources, NodeManager health, queue/user limits and other running applications. I would determine whether the application is waiting for resources before changing or killing anything.
